title: HelioBank x Redwood — Security Review (EU Data Residency)
summary: HelioBank security/compliance review focused on EU-only processing requirements for LLM inference workloads. Redwood walked through Hosted + Dedicated residency enforcement roadmap (region pinning, deterministic routing/no cross-region fallback by default, admission checks at gateway, downstream storage/logging enforcement) and how violations are handled (clear error codes + audit events). Customer asked about audit log fields/retention, SIEM export, exception process for temporary cross-region fallback during capacity events, and what is in/out of scope (historical artifacts migration is non-goal). Redwood committed to share sample audit event payloads, error code docs, and a short written statement on enforcement guarantees for beta/GA and exception approvals/expiry.
topics: EU-only processing requirement (no cross-region processing or storage)
Region pinning model (pinned_region vs allowed_regions) and precedence
Enforcement points (API gateway admission + routing + storage/logging)
Cross-region fallback behavior and capacity exhaustion handling
Audit logging (decision + violation events) and SIEM export
Error response contract and remediation guidance
Exception workflow (temporary allowance, approvals, expiry, audit evidence)
Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private/VPC considerations
questions: Can Redwood guarantee that prompts/completions and derived artifacts never leave the EU region when pinning is enabled?
What exactly is considered in-scope data for residency (traces, logs, analytics, request metadata)?
If there is a capacity incident in eu-west, will Redwood fail over to us-east automatically?
What audit events are emitted for allow/deny decisions, and what fields are included (tenant/org, region, reason, actor)?
What is the retention period for audit events and can they be exported to Splunk/Sentinel?
How do customers request a temporary exception and how is expiry enforced?
action_items: Kevin Osei - Send sample residency audit event payloads + SIEM export notes (Splunk/Sentinel) - due 2025-01-16
Marcus Lin - Share written summary of residency enforcement guarantees (Hosted/Dedicated) + exception workflow approvals/expiry - due 2025-01-17
Naomi Feldman - Confirm beta timeline for hosted data residency enforcement and what is included in Phase 1 vs Phase 2 - due 2025-01-17
Markus Klein - Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive on routing/failure modes with HelioBank platform team - due 2025-01-20
HelioBank (Anika Schulte) - Provide target regions and intended traffic patterns (SDK config, base URLs, expected volume) for pilot planning - due 2025-01-21
next_steps: Redwood to provide docs links: error code taxonomy for residency violations + audit events spec.
HelioBank to confirm whether they require strict fail-closed (deny) vs an approved exception path during capacity exhaustion.
Set up pilot plan: EU-pinned org/project, validate denial on non-EU endpoints, validate audit events in SIEM.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcription

Meeting: HelioBank x Redwood — Security Review (EU Data Residency)
Date: 2025-01-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood: Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering), Marcus Lin (Security Eng), Naomi Feldman (PM, Security & Compliance), Kevin Osei (Audit Log Export)
HelioBank: Sven Larsen (CISO), Marta Nowak (Head of Compliance), Anika Schulte (Platform Eng), Tomáš Dvořák (Security Architect)

Summary (auto)
- Discussed EU-only processing requirement and Redwood’s upcoming hosted data residency enforcement.
- Covered region pinning controls, enforcement points, audit logs, and exception handling.
- Agreed on follow-ups: sample audit events, written guarantee statement, technical deep dive.

Topics (auto)
- Data residency: definitions + enforcement
- Routing and failover
- Audit logging + SIEM export
- Error responses + troubleshooting
- Exceptions and approvals

Action items (auto)
- Redwood to send sample audit event payloads
- Redwood to share written enforcement summary + exception process
- Schedule technical deep dive

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making the time. I know this is a security review slash compliance review. The big thing we’ve been hearing is EU-only processing, no surprises, right.

[00:11] Sven Larsen: Yep. That’s it. If we turn this on and something ends up processed in the US, we’re basically dead.

[00:18] Markus Klein: Understood. Let me do quick intros. I’m Markus, solutions engineering. Marcus is our security engineering lead on this area. Naomi is product leading the residency program. Kevin is here because you asked specifically about audit logs and SIEM export.

[00:33] Marta Nowak: Hi.

[00:34] Anika Schulte: Hello.

[00:36] Tomáš Dvořák: Hi, thanks.

[00:39] Markus Klein: Great. Sven, do you want to give us the “what you need to be true” statement? Like, success criteria.

[00:46] Sven Larsen: Sure. We need contractual and technical assurance that prompts and completions—plus embeddings, metadata, logs—stay in the EU. Ideally one region. We also need evidence. Like audit trails we can show our regulator. And we need to know what happens in an outage. We don’t want automatic failover to a different geography.

[01:12] Markus Klein: Got it.

[01:13] Naomi Feldman: And just to frame: we have a project in flight called Hosted Data Residency Enforcement. The goal is region pinning controls and runtime enforcement. It’s not just “we have an EU region.” It’s “we stop the platform from doing cross-region things” unless explicitly allowed.

[01:30] Marta Nowak: When you say “things,” what counts? Like logs, traces, support access…?

[01:36] Marcus Lin: Good question. We typically break it down into: request content (prompt, messages, tool outputs), response content (completions), derived content (embeddings payloads, rerank inputs), and then operational artifacts: request metadata, metrics labels, logs, traces, audit logs, and any optional persistence features.

[01:58] Tomáš Dvořák: Optional persistence features meaning… storing prompts?

[02:01] Marcus Lin: Yeah. If you enable “store requests for replay” or longer retention debugging features—those are explicitly in scope for residency enforcement too. If you don’t enable them, we still have standard logs and traces, but we do not persist raw prompts by default in our standard tier. For enterprise features, we can configure retention and redaction.

[02:25] Anika Schulte: We’ll assume everything is in scope. We want a conservative answer.

[02:30] Naomi Feldman: That’s the right stance. So the enforcement model we’re implementing: you can set policy at org or project level like pinned_region="eu-west" or allowed_regions=["eu-west"]. When pinned is set, routing is deterministic—no cross-region fallback by default.

[02:51] Sven Larsen: Okay so if eu-west is down, requests fail?

[02:54] Naomi Feldman: With strict pinning, yes, the default behavior is “deny” rather than silently route elsewhere.

[03:00] Markus Klein: And it’s a clear error. Not like a 500.

[03:02] Naomi Feldman: Right—an explicit residency-related error code and message that tells you what to fix.

[03:08] Marta Nowak: I need to hear that again. You’re saying: no cross-region failover. You’d rather return an error.

[03:14] Naomi Feldman: Correct. Unless you explicitly configure an exception—like allowing cross-region fallback—and that would be recorded.

[03:23] Tomáš Dvořák: That exception is the thing that scares me. How is it controlled? Who can enable it?

[03:28] Marcus Lin: We’re building an exception workflow where it’s not something that a random developer toggles in production without oversight. It’s gated by permissions and, for regulated customers, we recommend an approval process. Also it’s time-bounded—expires automatically.

[03:45] Marta Nowak: Is that documented already?

[03:47] Marcus Lin: We have an internal spec and we can share the customer-facing process. It’s: request, security approval, GRC evidence, expiry enforcement.

[03:58] Kevin Osei: And the important part from an evidence standpoint: if an exception is granted, we emit audit events when it’s created and when it’s used. So you can show “this request was processed in region X due to exception Y approved by Z.”

[04:16] Anika Schulte: That’s helpful. But we’d like the default to be: we can’t even set it without, say, a compliance admin role.

[04:24] Markus Klein: Yep, RBAC for that.

[04:26] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. There’s a separate permission for managing residency settings.

[04:31] Sven Larsen: Let’s talk about enforcement. Where do you check it? Like in the gateway, in the model runtime, router?

[04:38] Naomi Feldman: It’s enforced at request admission in the API gateway before model execution. That’s important because it prevents any accidental processing. Then the router also respects the policy—so it won’t choose a region outside the pinned one. And we also enforce on downstream writes.

[04:59] Tomáš Dvořák: Downstream writes meaning logs and analytics pipelines. Those are the leaky parts.

[05:04] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[05:06] Kevin Osei: For example, audit logs, request logs, traces, usage/metering events—those have to stay in-region too. If the pipeline destination is misconfigured, we fail closed and emit an audit trail that says “write blocked due to residency policy.”

[05:24] Marta Nowak: Fail closed is good for compliance but bad for availability. So we need to understand the blast radius.

[05:31] Markus Klein: Totally. That’s a big part of how we roll it out—feature flags, canary, dashboards.

[05:37] Anika Schulte: Can you be specific about supported EU regions? We’re mainly eu-west-1 on AWS. But you’re not AWS only, right.

[05:45] Markus Klein: We support multiple cloud regions; for this conversation, the “EU West” region in our catalog maps to eu-west.

[05:53] Tomáš Dvořák: That’s vague. Is it Ireland? Frankfurt? Like actual geography matters.

[05:58] Markus Klein: Fair. For Hosted, we currently have EU capacity in Ireland. For Dedicated, we can do Ireland and Frankfurt depending on GPU availability. Naomi, correct me if I’m off.

[06:09] Naomi Feldman: That’s right. The region labels in the product are pinned to a specific cloud region. We can provide the mapping in writing for procurement/security questionnaire.

[06:21] Sven Larsen: Good, we’ll need that.

[06:23] Marta Nowak: Now, can you guarantee that “support” doesn’t pull data to the US? Like if someone opens a ticket.

[06:30] Marcus Lin: We have internal controls. But on the product side: we don’t require copying raw prompts into tickets. If you enable persistence features, those are stored in-region. For support, we can operate on metadata and audit logs. Also, access is audited.

[06:48] Tomáš Dvořák: But if your support staff are US-based, can they access EU data at rest?

[06:54] Marcus Lin: Access is controlled via RBAC and audited. For many customers we also do customer-managed keys in private deployments; for Hosted/Dedicated, keys are managed per region with KMS. We can talk about key management options; the residency program is primarily about region boundaries.

[07:14] Marta Nowak: Okay. We also need SIEM. We use Splunk now, moving some things to Sentinel.

[07:20] Kevin Osei: Great. Our audit log exporter supports both. We provide sample payloads and field mapping. For residency, there are specific event types like “residency.policy_evaluated” and “residency.violation.”

[07:34] Anika Schulte: What’s inside the payload? Like do you include the prompt?

[07:38] Kevin Osei: No raw prompt by default in audit logs. Audit logs are about “who did what” and “what decision was made.” For residency, the event includes org/project identifiers, requested region (if provided), evaluated pinned region, enforcement point (gateway/router/storage), decision allow/deny, and a reason code.

[07:57] Sven Larsen: Reason code meaning…

[07:59] Kevin Osei: Like “REGION_MISMATCH” or “CROSS_REGION_FALLBACK_BLOCKED.” (Names may differ slightly in final docs.)

[08:08] Naomi Feldman: And the API error response is aligned with that. We have machine readable error codes.

[08:14] Tomáš Dvořák: Can you give an example? Like what would the client see.

[08:18] Markus Klein: Sure. If you try to hit the US base URL with an EU-pinned org, you’ll get a 4xx with an error code like RESIDENCY_REGION_MISMATCH and it’ll say “Your organization is pinned to eu-west; send requests to https://api.eu-west.redwood… or update your SDK region.” Something like that.

[08:39] Anika Schulte: And this is before model execution?

[08:41] Naomi Feldman: Correct. It never reaches the model runtime.

[08:45] Marta Nowak: Do you log that error? Like can we see attempts.

[08:48] Kevin Osei: Yes, that generates an audit event and metrics counters. You can alert on violation spikes.

[08:58] Sven Larsen: That’s important. We need evidence of enforcement, but also detection if an app is misconfigured.

[09:04] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[09:06] Tomáš Dvořák: Let’s talk about “deterministic routing.” You mentioned smart routing. We’ve seen vendors say “EU-only” but then they do “hot standby” in the US.

[09:17] Naomi Feldman: We’re explicitly changing smart routing behavior when pinned. The router won’t pick a region outside pinned. There’s no “silent fallback” across geography.

[09:27] Sven Larsen: Even if you’re out of capacity?

[09:29] Naomi Feldman: Even then. You’ll get a capacity-related error, but it will still be in-region. If capacity is exhausted in-region, you get a “no capacity” response, not a cross-region execution.

[09:43] Markus Klein: There is an optional override, but again, it’s explicit and audited.

[09:49] Marta Nowak: The override: is it per request? Or per org?

[09:52] Naomi Feldman: We’re leaning per org/project policy with time bounds. Not per request header because that’s too easy to abuse.

[10:01] Tomáš Dvořák: Thank you.

[10:03] Anika Schulte: Is there a way to do allowed_regions as multiple EU regions? Like eu-west and eu-central, but not outside EU.

[10:10] Naomi Feldman: Yes, allowed_regions is a set. But we’d still recommend pinning for strictness. If you set allowed_regions with two regions, the router may choose either, but still within the set.

[10:23] Sven Larsen: That might be acceptable if both are EU. But we’d need to document that.

[10:29] Marta Nowak: And the logs would show which region processed it.

[10:32] Kevin Osei: Exactly. The audit events and request metadata include region.

[10:39] Tomáš Dvořák: And do you have data centers outside AWS? Like GCP.

[10:43] Markus Klein: We can run on multiple clouds. Residency is implemented at our control plane and runtime routing layer. So regardless of cloud, the region boundary is the enforcement unit.

[10:56] Anika Schulte: We also care about where you store “artifacts.” Like fine-tune datasets? Not sure if you do that.

[11:03] Markus Klein: For our platform, we’re primarily inference. If you use prompt logging, eval sets, or saved traces, those are artifacts. The current project you’re evaluating is specifically hosted inference residency. Naomi, do you want to clarify the non-goals?

[11:17] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Non-goal for initial release: automatic migration of existing historical artifacts. So residency enforcement applies from the point it’s enabled. We won’t move old data automatically as part of this feature.

[11:33] Marta Nowak: That means if we start fresh, we’re okay.

[11:36] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[11:38] Sven Larsen: What about retention? How long do you keep audit logs?

[11:42] Kevin Osei: Default retention depends on plan. For enterprise, we can do extended retention. Also, since you’re exporting to SIEM, you can retain as long as you need on your side.

[11:55] Tomáš Dvořák: Do you support immutable logs? Like WORM.

[11:59] Kevin Osei: We don’t do WORM storage as a product feature today, but we provide export streams so you can land it in your immutable store. We include event IDs and timestamps, and we sign events in transit in the sense of TLS; we can discuss integrity controls.

[12:18] Sven Larsen: Okay.

[12:20] Markus Klein: I want to make sure we address the big blocker: “Can Redwood provide an enforcement guarantee for EU-only?”

[12:28] Marcus Lin: From a technical perspective, with region pinning enabled, we enforce at gateway admission, router selection, and storage/logging writes. And we emit audit events for decisions/violations. That’s the enforcement guarantee.

[12:43] Marta Nowak: But we need wording.

[12:45] Marcus Lin: Understood. We’ll provide a written statement. It’ll include scope: what data types; what regions; and the behavior during misconfiguration or failover.

[12:57] Anika Schulte: Misconfiguration meaning if our SDK points at US endpoint.

[13:00] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. That’s a common one. We’re also improving SDK behavior to make region configuration more obvious and errors more actionable.

[13:11] Tomáš Dvořák: Will you allow specifying region in the SDK? Or it just uses base URL?

[13:15] Markus Klein: Both. In most SDKs you can set region or base URL. We’re standardizing that.

[13:23] Sven Larsen: And what if someone tries to override region per request header.

[13:27] Naomi Feldman: If you’re pinned, per-request “region hints” won’t move you out of the pinned region. They’re only hints within allowed set, and in strict mode they’re ignored if they conflict.

[13:41] Marta Nowak: Great.

[13:43] Kevin Osei: And we record “requested_region” in the audit event when present, so you can detect someone trying.

[13:51] Tomáš Dvořák: Nice.

[13:53] Markus Klein: Let’s talk exception handling because it keeps coming up. Sven, do you envision any scenario where you’d want to allow cross-region processing temporarily?

[14:03] Sven Larsen: Honestly, no. But the business might ask. If the EU region is down and our support center is on fire, they’ll ask “can we temporarily route to US.” We’d likely say no, but we need the policy.

[14:20] Marta Nowak: Even if we said yes, it must be time-limited and approved by compliance.

[14:24] Marcus Lin: That matches our design. The exception process requires approvals, it’s time-bounded, and usage is audited.

[14:33] Anika Schulte: Who approves on your side?

[14:35] Marcus Lin: Typically Security Engineering and GRC for evidence, depending on contract language.

[14:41] Naomi Feldman: And there’s also product controls to make sure it’s not just a hidden toggle.

[14:47] Tomáš Dvořák: Can exceptions be scoped to specific endpoints? Like only embeddings.

[14:52] Naomi Feldman: Not in the first iteration. We’re keeping it simple—policy is applied to request path generally. More granular scoping is a potential follow-on.

[15:04] Sven Larsen: That’s fine.

[15:06] Markus Klein: Another question we’ve gotten from banks: dedicated vs hosted. Anika, you’re evaluating hosted first, right?

[15:13] Anika Schulte: Yes. But Dedicated might be required later for throughput and isolation.

[15:18] Markus Klein: Dedicated supports the same residency controls. In Dedicated, it’s somewhat simpler because capacity is already in one region, but we still enforce so that analytics/logs don’t go elsewhere.

[15:32] Tomáš Dvořák: We’ll want that.

[15:34] Marta Nowak: We also have VPC requirements. Not now, but eventually.

[15:39] Markus Klein: That would be Redwood Private / VPC deployment. Residency there is mostly “your network boundary” and customer managed infra. But the policy model still applies.

[15:52] Sven Larsen: Okay.

[15:54] Marta Nowak: I want to ask about your certifications. SOC 2, ISO.

[15:58] Marcus Lin: We have SOC 2 Type II. ISO is in progress for some scopes. We can share the SOC report under NDA.

[16:07] Sven Larsen: We’ll need it.

[16:10] Markus Klein: Noted.

[16:12] Anika Schulte: Switching back to audit logs: can you include “who changed the residency setting” and “when” in the audit stream.

[16:20] Kevin Osei: Yes. Policy change events are audit logged, including actor, IP (when available), timestamp, and before/after values.

[16:31] Tomáš Dvořák: Before/after values includes region list.

[16:34] Kevin Osei: Correct.

[16:36] Marta Nowak: And do you have a dashboard for violations?

[16:39] Naomi Feldman: In the console, yes, we’re adding visibility into recent violations and a summary. Also internal dashboards for SRE.

[16:49] Sven Larsen: Can we access those dashboards via API?

[16:52] Naomi Feldman: We can expose violation summaries via API for enterprise. For now, the main integration is audit log export.

[17:02] Anika Schulte: That’s okay.

[17:04] Markus Klein: I saw in your notes you asked about “error messaging.” Brian on our side owns error contract but he’s not on the call. The basics: standardized HTTP status, machine code, doc link, and remediation guidance.

[17:18] Tomáš Dvořák: Doc link is good.

[17:20] Marta Nowak: But also: no data in the error.

[17:23] Markus Klein: Right. It won’t echo prompts.

[17:27] Sven Larsen: How do you prevent cross-region writes? Like what if your analytics backend is multi-region.

[17:34] Naomi Feldman: We’re implementing checks in the write path. If a component is configured to write to a non-compliant region, the operation is blocked and we produce an audit event. Also our infrastructure is being aligned so that region-specific pipelines stay region-specific.

[17:55] Tomáš Dvořák: That’s the right answer.

[17:58] Anika Schulte: I’d like to know if you do any “global” services like a global queue.

[18:04] Naomi Feldman: We avoid global queues for in-scope data paths. Control plane config is global but it stores policy, not payload. For payload-carrying systems, we partition by region.

[18:21] Marta Nowak: Control plane global—does that create residency risk?

[18:26] Marcus Lin: The key is what data is in the control plane. Residency policy and metadata are distinct from payload. For enterprise, we can be explicit about what’s stored where. And we keep audit logs region-scoped.

[18:43] Sven Larsen: We’ll want that in the documentation.

[18:46] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[18:48] Kevin Osei: I can send sample payloads for the residency audit events. You can see exactly what fields are included.

[18:55] Tomáš Dvořák: Please.

[18:56] Markus Klein: Great.

[18:59] Anika Schulte: One more: can you test that if we hit a US endpoint we get blocked.

[19:05] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We have end-to-end tests for that scenario. And in pilot we can validate with your org.

[19:13] Sven Larsen: Pilot timeline?

[19:15] Markus Klein: We can do a controlled pilot once the feature flag is enabled for your account. Naomi, what’s the rough beta window?

[19:23] Naomi Feldman: Beta is rolling; we’re onboarding a small set of enterprise accounts. We can target you in the next cohort, pending the paperwork.

[19:34] Marta Nowak: We need to see it before signing.

[19:37] Markus Klein: Understood.

[19:39] (crosstalk)

[19:40] Tomáš Dvořák: Sorry, one more nit: if a request is denied for residency, is it a 403?

[19:46] Markus Klein: Likely a 403 or 409 depending on contract. The important part is the machine code.

[19:52] Naomi Feldman: We’re standardizing on a consistent mapping. We’ll share the exact mapping in the error code doc.

[20:02] Sven Larsen: Okay.

[20:04] Markus Klein: Let’s see if there are any other blockers.

[20:07] Marta Nowak: We’ll need: (1) written statement of enforcement, (2) sample audit events, (3) SOC2 report, and (4) exception process documentation.

[20:18] Markus Klein: Great list.

[20:20] Marcus Lin: On exceptions, we’ll clarify that strict pinning has no fallback. The exception is opt-in, time-bounded, and requires elevated permissions.

[20:31] Anika Schulte: Also, can you clarify how “allowed_regions” interacts with “pinned_region.”

[20:36] Naomi Feldman: If pinned_region is set, it takes precedence. allowed_regions can exist but pinned is the effective constraint. If only allowed_regions is set, routing can choose any in the list.

[20:52] Tomáš Dvořák: Makes sense.

[20:53] Sven Larsen: Great.

[20:55] Markus Klein: Do you want to talk about competitors for context? We’ve seen Bedrock and Azure OpenAI used in banks.

[21:02] Sven Larsen: Yeah. We currently use Azure OpenAI for some internal protos but residency there is… complicated. Bedrock is on the list but we don’t like vendor lock-in. We’re looking at open models with strong serving. That’s why we’re here.

[21:19] Markus Klein: Got it.

[21:20] Anika Schulte: Another vendor said they’re EU-only but they still do US-based logging. That’s what we’re avoiding.

[21:28] Markus Klein: Understood.

[21:30] Naomi Feldman: That’s exactly why our project includes downstream write enforcement, not just routing.

[21:37] Kevin Osei: And audit evidence, so you don’t have to trust a slide.

[21:41] Marta Nowak: Good.

[21:44] Markus Klein: We’re at about half time. Any deeper questions around failure modes? Retries? SDK behavior?

[21:52] Tomáš Dvořák: Retries, yes. If your SDK retries, could it retry to a different region.

[21:58] Naomi Feldman: When pinned, retries remain within pinned region. The SDK may have multiple endpoints configured, but policy enforcement prevents cross-region. Also, we’re updating SDKs to surface residency errors as typed exceptions so you don’t accidentally auto-retry incorrectly.

[22:17] Anika Schulte: Typed exceptions is good.

[22:19] Sven Larsen: Okay.

[22:21] Markus Klein: For next steps, I propose: we schedule a technical deep dive with your platform team focusing on routing constraints and logging. And we send the artifacts Marta listed.

[22:33] Marta Nowak: Yes.

[22:34] Kevin Osei: I can send the audit event samples by Thursday.

[22:38] Marcus Lin: I’ll draft the enforcement/exception statement.

[22:42] Naomi Feldman: I’ll confirm the beta cohort timeline.

[22:45] Sven Larsen: Great.

[22:47] Markus Klein: Anything else before we wrap?

[22:50] Tomáš Dvořák: Just one: do you expose region in the response headers so we can log it.

[22:55] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we can include a response header like x-redwood-region or similar. We’ll confirm the exact header name.

[23:04] Anika Schulte: Perfect.

[23:06] Markus Klein: Alright, thank you everyone. We’ll follow up with the docs and scheduling.

[23:12] Sven Larsen: Thanks.

[23:13] Marta Nowak: Thank you.

[23:14] (call ends)

Note: Transcript may be incomplete; Fireflies sometimes truncates after meeting end due to recording stop.
